title: Boss: the retry storm postmortem
summary: A real-looking postmortem of a metastable outage: measure how long it outlived its trigger, show why the load stayed above capacity, and build the two action items: a retry budget and an adaptive concurrency limit.

steps.title: The postmortem: INC-4471, orders unavailable for 45 minutes
body: Blameless postmortem draft. Your job is the analysis section and the two action items.
SUMMARY   A schema migration locked a hot table for 3 minutes. Checkout failed for 45 minutes.
IMPACT    ~61% of checkout requests failed between 14:00 and 14:40.
14:00:00  trigger=off  errors=0.2%    normal: 6,000 rps, the orders DB handles about 8,000 rps
14:00:10  trigger=on   errors=3.0%    migration takes a lock on orders
14:00:40  trigger=on   errors=45.0%   api retries 3 attempts per request, no backoff, no budget
14:03:00  trigger=off  errors=52.0%   migration cancelled, lock released
14:40:40  trigger=off  errors=0.3%    gateway limit at 60% of traffic; DB drains
ACTION ITEMS  1. retry budget (10% of requests) in the API client
2. adaptive concurrency limit in front of the DB calls
The question the review will ask: *why did it not recover at 14:03?*

steps.title: How long did it outlive its trigger?
prompt: Write `int OutlivedSeconds(string[] lines)`. Each line is `HH:MM:SS trigger=on|off errors=N%` (the timeline
above, lines in time order).
- find the first line with `trigger=off` that comes **after** a `trigger=on` line: the trigger ended there;
- from that line on, find the first line with errors **below 1.0%**: recovery;
- return the seconds between them (`0` if it recovered on the same line);
- return `-1` when the trigger never turned on and off, or the errors never dropped below 1%.
hints: Split each line on spaces: the time, the trigger, the errors. `TimeSpan.Parse("14:03:00")` reads the time.
Two phases: first wait for an `on` followed by an `off`; then look for errors below 1, starting with that same `off` line.
template: Dojo.Eq("INC-4471 outlived its trigger by 37 min 40 s", 2260, OutlivedSeconds(dojoT));
Dojo.Eq("a healthy recovery takes 0 s", 0, OutlivedSeconds(new[] { "10:00:00 trigger=on errors=20.0%", "10:00:30 trigger=off errors=0.4%" }));
Dojo.Eq("a short tail", 50, OutlivedSeconds(new[] { "10:00:00 trigger=on errors=20.0%", "10:00:30 trigger=off errors=9.0%", "10:01:20 trigger=off errors=0.9%" }));
Dojo.Eq("never recovered in the data", -1, OutlivedSeconds(new[] { "10:00:00 trigger=on errors=20.0%", "10:00:30 trigger=off errors=30.0%" }));
Dojo.Eq("no trigger at all", -1, OutlivedSeconds(new[] { "10:00:00 trigger=off errors=0.1%", "10:00:30 trigger=off errors=0.2%" }));
Dojo.Eq("exactly 1.0% is not recovered yet", 60, OutlivedSeconds(new[] { "10:00:00 trigger=on errors=5.0%", "10:00:30 trigger=off errors=1.0%", "10:01:30 trigger=off errors=0.5%" }));

steps.title: Why it did not recover
prompt: Write `double OverloadFactor(double baseRps, double capacityRps, double errorRate, int attempts)`: the load the
database sees, divided by its capacity, when each request makes on average
`1 + p + p² + ... + p^(attempts-1)` calls with failure rate `p`. Round to 2 decimals.
At 14:03 the base traffic was 6,000 rps against 8,000 rps of capacity, errors were 52% and the API made up to
3 attempts: the factor is **1.34**, still over capacity although the base traffic is only 0.75 of it. So the
errors stay, so the retries stay. Without retries it would have been 0.75.
starter: double OverloadFactor(double baseRps, double capacityRps, double errorRate, int attempts)
solution: double OverloadFactor(double baseRps, double capacityRps, double errorRate, int attempts)
hints: This is `ExpectedCalls` from *Timeouts, deadlines and retries that help*, times the base traffic.
Divide by the capacity and round once at the end.
template: Dojo.Eq("a healthy system: retries cost nothing", 0.75, OverloadFactor(6000, 8000, 0, 3));
Dojo.Eq("14:20: more errors, more load", 1.49, OverloadFactor(6000, 8000, 0.61, 3));
Dojo.Eq("total failure: every attempt is used", 2.25, OverloadFactor(6000, 8000, 1, 3));

steps.title: Action item 1: a retry budget
prompt: Write a class `RetryBudget` that allows retries only up to a share of normal requests. Use whole numbers, so
no floating-point rounding creeps in: count in **hundredths of a retry**.
- `RetryBudget(int percent, int maxRetries)`: every request earns `percent` hundredths of a retry; the
budget holds at most `maxRetries` retries and **starts full**, so a short blip can still be retried;
- `void OnRequest()`: a normal (first-attempt) request was sent;
- `bool TryRetry()`: if a whole retry is in the budget, spend it and return true, else false.
With 10% and a maximum of 10: ten retries pass at once, the eleventh is refused, and after 20 more requests
two more retries are allowed.
solution: public void OnRequest() => balance = Math.Min(max, balance + percent);
hints: Keep a balance in hundredths: a retry costs 100, a request adds `percent`, and the cap is `maxRetries × 100`.
Start the balance at the cap.
template: for (var i = 0; i < 15; i++) if (dojoRb.TryRetry()) dojoBurst++;
Dojo.Eq("the full budget allows 10 retries", 10, dojoBurst);
Dojo.Check("20 requests at 10% earn retry one", dojoRb.TryRetry());
Dojo.Check("nine requests are not enough for a retry", !dojoRb.TryRetry());
for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) if (dojoCap.TryRetry()) dojoAfter++;
Dojo.Eq("the budget never grows past its maximum", 2, dojoAfter);

steps.title: Action item 2: an adaptive concurrency limit
prompt: A fixed limit is wrong on the day the database slows down. An **AIMD** limit (additive increase,
multiplicative decrease, the same idea as TCP congestion control) adapts:
Write a class `AimdLimit`:
- `AimdLimit(int initial, int min, int max)` and `int Limit`;
- `void OnResult(double latencyMs, double targetMs, bool dropped)`:
- `dropped` (a timeout or an error): halve the limit (`Limit / 2`);
- otherwise slower than `targetMs`: shrink to 90% (`Limit * 9 / 10`, whole numbers);
- otherwise: grow by 1;
- always keep it between `min` and `max`.
From 20 (min 5, max 100): three fast results make it 23, a slow one 20, a drop 10.
starter: public AimdLimit(int initial, int min, int max) { }
public void OnResult(double latencyMs, double targetMs, bool dropped) { }
solution: public AimdLimit(int initial, int min, int max)
public int Limit { get; private set; }
public void OnResult(double latencyMs, double targetMs, bool dropped)
var next = dropped ? Limit / 2 : latencyMs > targetMs ? Limit * 9 / 10 : Limit + 1;
hints: Compute the next value with a nested conditional: dropped, then slow, then fast.
`Math.Clamp(next, min, max)` keeps it in range (and fixes an initial value outside it).
template: dojoL.OnResult(12, 50, false); dojoL.OnResult(15, 50, false); dojoL.OnResult(20, 50, false);
for (var i = 0; i < 200; i++) dojoL.OnResult(10, 50, false);
Dojo.Eq("exactly on target counts as fast", 6, new Func<int>(() => { var x = new AimdLimit(5, 1, 10); x.OnResult(50, 50, false); return x.Limit; })());
Dojo.Eq("an initial value outside the range is clamped", 100, new AimdLimit(500, 5, 100).Limit);
